fetched_contents.text: Electrochemical sensing of human hormones Endocrine glands have the endocrine cells for the synthesis and secretion of hormones. They are transported to target tissues through the circulatory system, performing several function by binding to their specific receptors. Hormones assist in coordinating metabolic tasks, i.e., growth, development, maturation, survival, and reproduction [1,2]. An imbalance in hormone levels may cause diseases [3], e.g., hypo- and hyperthyroidism by the deficiency and excess of T3 and T4 [4], diabetes mellitus by insulin deficiency, and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and amenorrhea by luteinizing hormone (LH) dysregulation [5]. Sensitive sensors can better detect hormones because of their smaller concentrations in the human body. They are detected via the biorecognition elements such as enzymes or antibodies [3] (see Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, Table 4, Table 5, Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6, Fig. 7, Fig. 8, Fig. 9). Several diagnostic techniques are available for early disease diagnosis through biomarkers. The conventional ones include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), capillary electrophoresis (CE), localized surface plasma resonance, radioimmunoassay (RIA), immunoradiometric assay (IRMA), fluorescence immunoassay, and immunochemiluminescent assay (ICMA) [[84], [179],10]. These techniques are time-consuming, require trained personnel, and involve multistage processing. One of the diagnostic techniques is biosensing via the biosensors [3]. Biosensors are the clinical, environmental, and food monitoring tools to detect biological and chemical components [1]. Biosensor components include bio-recognition elements and a tiny transducer. They have inexpensive, smaller, faster response rates and user-friendly attributes. On the basis of transduction methods, biosensors are classified as piezoelectric, electrochemical, and optical. Biosensors detect biomarkers specific to a disease, such as allergy, cancer, and heart attack. Electrochemical biosensors transform chemical signals into analytical signals. They have the characteristics of response time, linear concentration range, selectivity, sensitivity, regeneration etc. They operate via a chemical reaction taking place between immobilized molecules and target compounds, involving electrons affecting the analytes' electrical properties. The electrochemical transducers include impedimetric biosensors which measure impedance of medium present between the electrodes. Amperometric biosensors measure current, potentiometric measure generated potential, and conductiometric measure conductivity [3]. The sensors and biosensors use nanomaterials to increase surface area, promote catalysis [10], and amplify the electrochemical signals [25]. Immunosensors for hormone detection possess high selectivity and sensitivity because of the interaction between antigen and antibody. An electrochemical transducer measures the signal. Depending on signal type, they are classified as potentiometric, conductometric, impedimetric, and amperometric immunosensors. Immunosensors are used in clinical and bioanalytical fields [180] to detect biomolecules [181]. One of the electroanalytical techniques is voltammetry, which involves cyclic voltammetry (CV), differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), square-wave voltammetry (SWV), and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) [182]. CV is an electrochemical analysis technique [183], employed to measure current responses of redox reactions involving molecular species and to study catalysis [184]. Three-terminal electrode cell configuration i.e., a counter electrode, a reference electrode, and a working electrode to execute CV measurements. The current response of working electrode is measured by applying voltage to the sample [185]. This procedure is repeated several times to attain a plot known as a cyclic voltammogram. CV thus explores the redox status. For example, employed in research and industry to study the antioxidant status of animals and humans [185], drug quality in pharmaceuticals, and determination of biomolecules [185]. Differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) evaluates compounds at trace levels, with high sensitivity [186], due to its discrimination of faradaic currents. In DPV, the potential perturbation, which comprises of small pulses, is superimposed upon a staircase waveform [187]. Peak potentials of DPV have a constant increase in rectangular pulses and are employed in slow reaction kinetics and irreversible systems [182]. Square wave voltammetry (SWV), is an ideal technique for species detection at low concentrations, and can characterize unknown compounds in solution by evaluating the number of electrons exchanged in a chemical reaction, and by analyzing the electrochemical potential [188]. Peak potentials constantly increase square oscillations and are used for reversible and rapid reaction kinetic systems [182]. In linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), the stationary working electrode is dipped in the electrolyte solution to repress the charged migration of reactants and products. The electroactive species are transferred from and to the electrode surface by diffusion, and the working electrode's potential is altered linearly with time. This starts from potential with no electrode reaction to the point where redox occurs [189]. This review summarizes electrochemical biosensors for hormone monitoring. fetched_contents.text: Consideration of Sample Matrix Effects and “Biological” Noise in Optimizing the Limit of Detection of Biosensors In athletics, the time to run a set distance serves the purpose of quantitatively comparing the performance of runners. In analytical sciences, we are very familiar with reporting the limit of detection, which oftentimes serves as that comparative measure in performance (it is not the only one, but surely the most common). In sensing (and at ACS Sensors), we aim for the widespread use of sensors in a series of significant applications (clinical, medical, biological, environmental, or industrial) that will help humanity. As such, we strive to perfect, optimize, calibrate, and benchmark our sensors to reach the best performance for an analyte. Coming back to the running analogy, we cannot assume that a sprinter will run as fast in the mud (or since winter is coming, snow for us up north!), where the feet sink deep and slip on the surface, than on an Olympic track, where the runner’s feet bounce smoothly off the track to gain speed. Performance depends on the environment where it is measured. This also applies to sensors. In sensing, we therefore need to compare the limit of detection in a realistic environment for the intended purpose and calculate it in an appropriate manner. (1) Achieving the lowest limit of detection in the ideal conditions of a clean laboratory samples is far from a guarantee of success in a clinical sample. To further advance the usefulness of sensors and the field in general, we need to ask ourselves: What happens to the performance or limit of detection when biosensors are exposed to clinical samples? Addressing this question will also explain why we place such an emphasis on analyzing “real” samples (i.e., in biofluids) at ACS Sensors. Let us first look at the basics. The common equation for the limit of detection (3σ/m, where σ is the standard deviation and m is the sensitivity of the method) is rather simple in appearance (one can either increase the sensitivity or decrease the noise) but can be deceptively complex once we try to optimize the limit of detection. It is fairly common to optimize the limit of detection by optimizing the components involved in the sensor in ideal conditions to improve sensitivity (we receive a number of papers focusing on this aspect). This can be achieved from the material chemistry (i.e., composition, shape, or size of a nanomaterial), with changes in the recognition element (i.e., a new aptamer, fluorophore, or antibody, among others), or a new sensing scheme using amplified response (i.e., secondary assays, enzymatic amplification, among others). This is where the field devotes the most effort. However, let us look at the noise, which might be arguably the most important term in the equation, but somewhat overlooked. To reduce the noise of a sensor, some will optimize the hardware, including electronics, optics, or other instrumental consideration, and others the software, including chemometric data processing, machine learning approaches, or other signal processing methods. While these aspects are important to consider in a biosensor, oftentimes these are also optimized in ideal conditions using clean laboratory samples, but noise can also come from the biological sample matrix or the environment of the measurement. As such, it is important to introduce a significant nuance between the instrumental limit of detection and the method’s limit of detection. The former is the limit of detection obtained for the analyte in a pure solution. This is the best-case scenario, but unlikely to be encountered by actual sensors (and oftentimes the one reported in research articles). As such, the method’s limit of detection is more appropriate in biosensing. To determine the method’s limit of detection, the analyte must be measured in the actual matrix of intended use and all sample preparation steps must be performed. While in appearance simple, one will often find that biology “does not cooperate” as much as physics, chemistry, or engineering. Summarized in one statement, a lot can go wrong with biological samples! The uncertainty of a measurement often increases when biomolecules are involved in the sensing mechanism and sensor-to-sensor reproducibility suffers in comparison to their chemical counterpart. Expectedly, the method’s limit of detection is at higher concentrations than the instrumental limit of detection. The sources of divergence between the two limits of detection are numerous but can be understood from the lower than 100% recovery rate of the analyte following sample preparation methods, matrix effects, and the presence of interference, among others. This “biological” noise can cause significant headaches to the researchers involved in the development of biosensors, and the author of this editorial personally sympathizes with anyone in this position. A comprehensive overview of the sources of “biological” noise is beyond the scope of this editorial. Instead, a few common sources of “biological” noise affecting the output of a sensor are discussed here for the reader’s consideration in their sensor design and optimization. The sample matrix might be one of the largest contributors to the “biological” noise. The matrix effect can be manifested in several ways. One of the common effects in a complex matrix is the interaction of the analyte with molecules in the matrix. Hence, the question is whether the analyte is free or bound in the biofluid and is the bound analyte detected with the same sensitivity or not. This important factor will change the sensitivity of the sensor for the analyte. While one can expect that this effect will be detrimental to the sensitivity, if the bound analyte remains detected by the sensor and the sensor is mass or size sensitive, the sensitivity can actually increase in the biofluid. fetched_contents.text: A Comparative Study of a Multi-Method Electrochemical Biosensor for Rapid Detection of Microcystins in Treated Wastewater Nearly third of the world population lack access to safe drinking water, as recently been reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), in a Joint Monitoring Program (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene.1 Water sources are vulnerable not only to anthropogenic pollutants but also to natural toxins produced during harmful cyanobacterial blooms (HCBs). HCBs are a major threat to managing open water bodies used for aquaculture, drinking, and recreation. Globally, water contamination resulting from cyanobacteria blooms has been reported in lakes, lagoons, oceans, rivers, streams, water reservoirs, and wells.2–7 Eutrophication and climate change are known drivers of HCBs proliferation, and the number of affected lakes is expected to increase by at least 20% globally by 2050.1,8,9 Cyanotoxins (CTXs), particularly Microcystins (MCs), produced during HCBs pose significant environmental and health risks, contaminating freshwater, brackish, and saltwater systems, and also groundwater, reclaimed water and treated wastewater reservoirs.10–12 Microcystins, known for their hepatotoxic effects, are subject to regulatory monitoring, with stringent guidelines established by organizations like the WHO, which recommends a guideline limit of 1 μg L−1 in drinking water.13 Current detection methods include analytical techniques such as chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry or UV detection, and immunoassays such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and protein phosphatase inhibition assays.2,14 Among these, ELISA is widely used due to its sensitivity and selectivity,15,16 but it remains time-consuming, requires specialized equipment, and is unsuitable for rapid on-site monitoring,2,17 emphasizing the need for faster, portable, and cost-effective alternatives, especially in resource-limited settings. Electrochemical biosensors (ECBs) have emerged as promising solutions to overcome these limitations. ECBs offer a rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective solution with a potential for miniaturization, enabling real-time monitoring of water quality.17–21 By coupling the selectivity of biological recognition elements with the sensitivity of EC transduction, ECBs can detect small target analytes at ultra-low concentrations.17,22 Various EC techniques have been applied for cyanotoxin detection using ECBs, demonstrating their potential for cyanotoxin detection,17,20,21,23,24 including label-free electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)25–27 and amperometric methods.23,28,29 Amperometric biosensors are based on electron transfer reactions, specifically, the oxidation or reduction of electroactive species on the electrode surface. When a fixed potential is applied, these reactions generate current changes that can be measured to quantify the analyte.17,20 Amperometric detection is particularly effective in systems with mass transfer, such as flow electrode systems or rotating/vibrating electrodes, and is effective in monitoring enzyme reactions in biocatalytic biosensors.17,30,31 EIS-based (immuno-impedimetric) biosensors, on the other hand, detect target toxins through changes in the impedance of an electrode surface modified with specific recognition elements (e.g., antibodies, nucleic acids, or receptors), enabling highly sensitive detection at low concentrations.32–34 For impedance measurements, a small sinusoidal potential is applied between the working and counter electrodes, and the resulting current is analyzed. The in-phase and out-of-phase components correspond to the real (resistive) and imaginary (capacitive) elements, respectively.33,35,36 Immuno-impedimetric biosensors have demonstrated very low detection limits in surface-based immunodetection. Typically, antigen binding to an antibody-functionalized electrode impedes the electron transfer of a redox probe, resulting in an increase in charge transfer resistance (RCT).27 Amperometric immunoassays, by contrast, measure the current generated by electroactive species at a fixed potential, with the signal proportional to analyte concentration. Unlike EIS, which directly detects the target analyte, substrate-mediated amperometric detection is an indirect method, functioning as an electrochemical analogue to ELISA. In faradaic EIS, an alternating potential is applied across a range of frequencies and the current response is measured, whereas amperometric techniques apply a constant potential and measure the resulting current over time.37–39 Both methods have shown significant promise in environmental diagnostics, including CTX detection. Although previous studies have detected MCs using either approach alone,32,34,40,41 this study is the first to integrate both techniques on a similar chip. Collectively, combining these two EC techniques can enhance the selectivity, sensitivity, and practical utility of ECBs across diverse applications, including environmental diagnostics. Herein, we present a comparative evaluation of immuno-impedimetric and substrate-mediated amperometric detection modes, implemented by a multi-method ECB for rapid and accurate quantification of MCs in water. We hypothesized that the combination of the two EC methods can enhance the selectivity, sensitivity, and overall utility of ECBs in quantitative detection of MCs. The working electrodes of the developed miniaturized biochip were functionalized with specific anti-microcystin antibodies or with immobilized toxins, designed for on-site analysis of MCs. The performance of the ECB was evaluated against ELISA, with a detailed comparison of sensitivity, LOD, dynamic range, run time, and usability. Building on our previous work42,43 where we developed an EIS-based immunosensor capable of detecting MCs at concentrations as low as 3 ng L−1 (3 ppt) and was compared to ELISA for detecting MCs in treated waste…

Electrochemical immunosensors for hormone detection are structured around a combination of a biorecognition layer and an electrochemical transducer, with the overall architecture enabling selective and sensitive detection through antigen-antibody interaction [N1-F1]. The sensor platform typically includes a working electrode, counter electrode, and reference electrode, with the working electrode being the site of redox signal generation [N1-F1]. The transducer types used most commonly are amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, and impedimetric biosensors, with voltammetric techniques such as differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), square-wave voltammetry (SWV), and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) also widely used for signal acquisition [N1-F1]. A separate review also emphasizes that amperometric and impedimetric biosensors are the two important types classified by their DC and AC operation, and that printed electrochemical biosensors are an important area of development with opportunities in transducing principles and metrological characteristics [N4-R1][N4-R4].

Antibody/antigen orientation and immobilization strategies are central to sensor function. The review on ACTH detection describes oriented immobilization of anti-ACTH antibodies using amino phenylboronic acid on screen-printed carbon modified electrodes, which is important for controlling antibody orientation and improving recognition efficiency [N3-F4]. The same paper also notes that electrografting of aryldiazonium species is used for linkage between the electrochemical transducer surface and biosensor recognition elements, and that this method enables covalent immobilization of biomolecules in a stable and reproducible way [N3-F4]. The evidence further indicates that immobilization strategies can be tailored to the recognition element, including antibodies, enzymes, DNA, aptamers, peptides, and whole cells, and that aryldiazonium-derived layers can be used to attach nanomaterials and other components for more sophisticated sensing layers [N3-F4]. In addition, the broader electrochemical sensing review notes that biosensor components include bio-recognition elements and a tiny transducer, and that nanomaterials are used to increase surface area, promote catalysis, and amplify electrochemical signals [N1-F1].

Signal generation and detection mechanism depend on the transducer type. Amperometric biosensors measure current changes resulting from electron transfer reactions, specifically the oxidation or reduction of electroactive species at a fixed potential [N6-F3]. In the electrochemical context, the signal can be generated indirectly, such as in substrate-mediated amperometric detection, where the current is proportional to analyte concentration [N6-F3]. Impedimetric biosensors, by contrast, detect changes in impedance between working and counter electrodes, with the in-phase and out-of-phase components corresponding to resistive and capacitive elements respectively [N6-F3]. Voltammetric methods such as DPV and SWV are used because they can achieve high sensitivity and are effective for trace-level detection, while LSV is used to study diffusion-controlled redox reactions [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that biosensors operate via a chemical reaction between immobilized molecules and target compounds, involving electrons affecting the analytes’ electrical properties [N1-F1]. Overall, the sensor architecture combines a selective recognition layer with a transducer that converts biochemical interaction into an electrochemical signal, with the choice of transducer and immobilization strategy shaping both sensitivity and specificity [N1-F1][N3-F4].

Analytical performance in electrochemical immunoassays is measured by several interrelated metrics. Sensitivity is defined as the ability of a method to discriminate between small concentration differences, while detection limit is the minimum amount detectable with a certain level of confidence [N2-R3][N2-R4]. Dynamic range refers to the concentration range over which the response remains linear, and the literature explicitly highlights that a tunable dynamic sensing range can be achieved in electrochemical aptasensors [N2-R1]. The evidence also indicates that sensitivity can be improved by optimizing components such as nanomaterials, recognition elements, or amplified response schemes, while noise reduction can come from hardware optimization, software processing, chemometric methods, or machine learning [N5-F2]. This makes the method’s limit of detection particularly important in biosensing, because it should be determined in the actual matrix of intended use rather than just in ideal conditions [N5-F2].

Selectivity and cross-reactivity are important because electrochemical biosensors can be affected by nonspecific interactions and matrix effects. The matrix effect can reduce access of redox molecules to the sensor and lower sensitivity, while nonspecific interactions can cause interference [N5-R1]. The same source also emphasizes that the method’s limit of detection can be higher than the instrumental limit of detection because of recovery rate, matrix effects, and interference [N5-F2]. In addition, the comparative study of electrochemical biosensors notes that immuno-impedimetric biosensors can demonstrate very low detection limits in surface-based immunodetection, and that amperometric detection can be an indirect method analogous to ELISA [N6-F3]. This implies that selectivity is not only a matter of the recognition element itself, but also of the overall biosensor design and matrix compatibility.

Reproducibility, stability, and assay time are also central. The review on biosensors notes that sensor-to-sensor reproducibility can suffer compared to chemical counterparts, and that biological samples can introduce uncertainty and variability [N5-F2]. Stability is related to the sensor’s performance over time and under operating conditions, though the evidence here is more explicitly about reproducibility and matrix effects than about long-term stability. Assay time is relevant because biosensors can be rapid and miniaturized, and the comparative study specifically notes that electrochemical biosensors offer a rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective solution with potential for miniaturization and real-time monitoring [N6-F3]. The review on biosensor metrology also emphasizes opportunities in transducing principles and metrological characteristics, which suggests that assay performance can be optimized through both hardware and signal-processing approaches [N4-R4].

Taken together, the evidence points to a core tradeoff: analytical performance is measured in terms of sensitivity, detection limit, dynamic range, selectivity, and reproducibility, but these metrics are often influenced by the matrix, the choice of transducer, and the optimization of signal processing and biosensor design [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-F2][N6-F3]. The method’s limit of detection is especially meaningful in practice because it must be evaluated in the intended use matrix rather than in ideal, clean samples [N5-F2].

Electrochemical biosensors are generally compared to established immunoassays such as ELISA on the basis of sensitivity, selectivity, detection limit, dynamic range, run time, usability, and practical implementation [N6-F3]. The comparative study of a multi-method electrochemical biosensor for microcystins in treated wastewater reports that both ECB methods demonstrated comparable sensitivity and enhanced reliability relative to conventional ELISA, while also emphasizing that ECBs offer rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective solutions with miniaturization potential [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The same study also notes that ELISA is widely used for its sensitivity and selectivity, but it remains time-consuming, requires specialized equipment, and is unsuitable for rapid on-site monitoring, which highlights a key practical limitation of conventional immunoassays [N6-F3]. In addition, the comparative study explicitly compares immuno-impedimetric and substrate-mediated amperometric detection modes, indicating that electrochemical biosensors can be designed to combine multiple EC techniques to improve selectivity and practical utility [N6-F3].

The practical limitations of electrochemical biosensors include matrix effects, biological noise, and the difficulty of translating ideal performance into real-world use. The sample matrix effect evidence states that the method’s limit of detection is often higher than the instrumental limit of detection because of recovery rate, matrix effects, and interference, and that biological samples can introduce significant noise and variability [N5-F2]. It also explains that the matrix can affect analyte availability and that biological samples are difficult to control compared to clean laboratory conditions [N5-F2]. The comparative study likewise notes that ECBs must be evaluated in the actual matrix of intended use, and that biosensors are often optimized in ideal conditions but may not perform as well in real samples [N6-F3]. This means that electrochemical biosensors are not automatically superior in every setting; their performance depends on the matrix, sample preparation, and the presence of interferences [N5-F2][N6-F3].

Tradeoffs between performance and complexity are clear. Electrochemical biosensors can be rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective, but they often require careful electrode design, immobilization strategies, and signal-processing approaches to maintain selectivity and reproducibility [N4-R4][N6-F3]. The evidence also shows that more complex transducers such as impedimetric or voltammetric systems can improve sensitivity and dynamic range, but they may also increase assay time and the need for specialized instrumentation [N1-F1][N4-R3]. The comparative study’s emphasis on combining immuno-impedimetric and amperometric modes suggests that complexity can be traded against broader utility and robustness [N6-F3]. Overall, the evidence indicates that electrochemical biosensors can match or exceed ELISA in sensitivity and offer advantages in speed and portability, but they face real-world limitations from matrix effects, biological noise, and the need for robust sensor design and signal processing [N6-F3][N5-F2].

The hormone-specific design and performance evidence for estradiol, testosterone, and ACTH shows that each hormone requires tailored recognition strategies and sensor configurations. For estradiol, the evidence points to antibody biosensors based on competitive mechanisms and to the use of different bioreceptors, with competitive immunosensors excelling in estradiol detection [N3-R2]. The comparative study on electrochemical biosensors also frames hormone detection in a broader context of recognition elements, signal-sensing methods, and signal amplification, suggesting that estradiol detection is influenced by both antibody format and signal-processing choices [N3-R2][N7-R2]. A separate review notes that 17β-estradiol biosensors include different bioreceptors and that aptamer-based sensors can show improved LOD and detection range [N7-R1][N7-R4]. For testosterone, the evidence includes a reported electrochemical immunosensor with a limit of detection of 1.7 pg/mL and a linear detection range from 5×10⁻³ to 50 ng/mL, with an r² value of 0.995, and a magnetic bead-based screen-printed carbon electrode design [N3-R3]. For ACTH, the evidence reports an ultrasensitive electrochemical immunosensor with an extremely low detection limit of 18 pg/L, competitive immunoassay design, and evaluation against other hormones such as cortisol, estradiol, testosterone, progesterone, hGH, and prolactin [N3-F4].

Sample preparation and matrix challenges are especially important across all three hormones. The matrix effect evidence explains that biological samples can restrict access to redox molecules, lower sensitivity, and introduce nonspecific interactions and interference [N5-R1]. The same source also notes that the method’s limit of detection is affected by recovery rate, matrix effects, and interference, and that biological samples are harder to control than clean laboratory conditions [N5-F2]. The comparative study on microcystins in treated wastewater likewise emphasizes that ECBs must be evaluated in the actual matrix of intended use and that biosensors are often optimized in ideal conditions but may not perform equally well in real samples [N6-F3]. For hormone detection, this means that sample preparation is not merely a preprocessing step; it can significantly alter the observed LOD, selectivity, and reproducibility [N5-F2][N6-F3].

The hormone-specific requirements differ in part because of the physicochemical properties of the analyte and the matrix in which it is found. Estradiol detection often benefits from competitive immunoassay formats and aptamer-based strategies, which may help overcome matrix interference and improve LOD and range [N3-R2][N7-R4]. Testosterone is reported with a very low detection limit in the picogram-per-milliliter range, suggesting a design optimized for low-concentration detection and a linear range that spans several orders of magnitude [N3-R3]. ACTH detection is reported with an even lower detection limit of 18 pg/L and excellent selectivity against other hormones, indicating that orientation and cross-reactivity control are especially important for this hormone [N3-F4]. Overall, the evidence suggests that hormone-specific design must account for sensitivity, selectivity, matrix compatibility, and assay robustness, with the choice of antibody format, immobilization strategy, and detection method being strongly hormone-dependent [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F4].

## Main features and analytical performance characteristics of electrochemical hormone immunoassays

Electrochemical immunosensors for hormone detection are designed to combine the specificity of antigen–antibody recognition with the sensitivity and miniaturization potential of electrochemical transduction [N1-F1][N6-F3]. Their main features can be summarized as follows:

1. **Sensor architecture: biorecognition layer + electrochemical transducer**  
   The sensor typically consists of a biorecognition layer, where antibodies or other biomolecules are immobilized to recognize the target hormone, and an electrochemical transducer that converts the biochemical interaction into an electrical signal [N1-F1][N3-F4]. The transducer can be amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, or impedimetric, with voltammetric methods such as differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), square-wave voltammetry (SWV), and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) also widely used [N1-F1][N6-F3]. A separate review emphasizes that amperometric and impedimetric biosensors are the two main types classified by DC and AC operation, and that printed electrochemical biosensors are an important area of development with opportunities in transducing principles and metrological characteristics [N4-R1][N4-R4].

2. **Antibody/antigen orientation and immobilization**  
   Immobilization strategy is central to sensor function. The evidence shows that antibodies can be oriented and immobilized using coupling agents such as amino phenylboronic acid, which helps control antibody orientation and improve recognition efficiency [N3-F4]. Electrografting of aryldiazonium species is also used to link biosensor recognition elements to the electrode surface, enabling stable and reproducible covalent immobilization of biomolecules [N3-F4]. This means that the choice of immobilization method directly affects both specificity and signal quality [N1-F1][N3-F4].

3. **Signal generation and detection mechanism**  
   Amperometric biosensors measure current changes resulting from electron transfer reactions, typically at a fixed potential [N6-F3]. Impedimetric biosensors detect changes in impedance between working and counter electrodes, with the signal split into resistive and capacitive components [N6-F3]. Voltammetric methods are especially useful for trace detection because they can achieve high sensitivity and are effective for low-concentration analytes [N1-F1]. Overall, the sensor architecture is designed to convert a biochemical interaction into an electrochemical signal that can be measured and interpreted [N1-F1][N6-F3].

---

## Analytical performance characteristics

### Sensitivity, detection limit, and dynamic range  
Electrochemical immunoassays are evaluated by sensitivity, detection limit, and dynamic range. ## Main features and analytical performance characteristics of electrochemical hormone immunoassays

Electrochemical immunosensors for hormone detection are designed to combine the specificity of antigen–antibody recognition with the sensitivity and miniaturization potential of electrochemical transduction [N1-F1][N6-F3]. Their main features can be summarized as follows:

1. **Sensor architecture: biorecognition layer + electrochemical transducer**  
   The sensor typically consists of a biorecognition layer, where antibodies or other biomolecules are immobilized to recognize the target hormone, and an electrochemical transducer that converts the biochemical interaction into an electrical signal [N1-F1][N3-F4]. The transducer can be amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, or impedimetric, with voltammetric methods such as differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), square-wave voltammetry (SWV), and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) also widely used [N1-F1][N6-F3]. A separate review emphasizes that amperometric and impedimetric biosensors are the two main types classified by DC and AC operation, and that printed electrochemical biosensors are an important area of development with opportunities in transducing principles and metrological characteristics [N4-R1][N4-R4].

2. **Antibody/antigen orientation and immobilization**  
   Immobilization strategy is central to sensor function. The evidence shows that antibodies can be oriented and immobilized using coupling agents such as amino phenylboronic acid, which helps control antibody orientation and improve recognition efficiency [N3-F4]. Electrografting of aryldiazonium species is also used to link biosensor recognition elements to the electrode surface, enabling stable and reproducible covalent immobilization of biomolecules [N3-F4]. This means that the choice of immobilization method directly affects both specificity and signal quality [N1-F1][N3-F4].

3. **Signal generation and detection mechanism**  
   Amperometric biosensors measure current changes resulting from electron transfer reactions, typically at a fixed potential [N6-F3]. Impedimetric biosensors detect changes in impedance between working and counter electrodes, with the signal split into resistive and capacitive components [N6-F3]. Voltammetric methods are especially useful for trace detection because they can achieve high sensitivity and are effective for low-concentration analytes [N1-F1]. Overall, the sensor architecture is designed to convert a biochemical interaction into an electrochemical signal that can be measured and interpreted [N1-F1][N6-F3].

## Analytical performance characteristics

### Selectivity and cross-reactivity  
Selectivity is a key performance characteristic because electrochemical biosensors can be affected by nonspecific interactions and matrix effects. The matrix effect can restrict access of redox molecules to the sensor and lower sensitivity, while nonspecific interactions can cause interference [N5-R1]. The same source also notes that the method’s limit of detection can be higher than the instrumental limit of detection because of recovery rate, matrix effects, and interference [N5-F2]. ## Comparison with established assay methods and practical limitations

Electrochemical biosensors are generally compared to established immunoassays such as ELISA on the basis of sensitivity, selectivity, detection limit, dynamic range, run time, usability, and practical implementation [N6-F3]. There are clear tradeoffs between performance and complexity. Electrochemical immunosensors for hormones such as estradiol, testosterone, and ACTH are highly selective and sensitive because they rely on antigen–antibody recognition and electrochemical signal transduction [N1-F1].    Immobilization strategy is central to sensor function. ## Main features and analytical performance characteristics of electrochemical hormone immunoassays

Electrochemical immunosensors for hormone detection are designed to combine the specificity of antigen–antibody recognition with the sensitivity and miniaturization potential of electrochemical transduction [N1-F1][N6-F3]. Their main features can be summarized as follows:

1. **Sensor architecture: biorecognition layer + electrochemical transducer**  
   The sensor typically consists of a biorecognition layer, where antibodies or other biomolecules are immobilized to recognize the target hormone, and an electrochemical transducer that converts the biochemical interaction into an electrical signal [N1-F1][N3-F4]. The transducer can be amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, or impedimetric, with voltammetric methods such as differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), square-wave voltammetry (SWV), and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) also widely used [N1-F1][N6-F3]. A separate review emphasizes that amperometric and impedimetric biosensors are the two main types classified by DC and AC operation, and that printed electrochemical biosensors are an important area of development with opportunities in transducing principles and metrological characteristics [N4-R1][N4-R4].

2. **Antibody/antigen orientation and immobilization**  
   Immobilization strategy is central to sensor function. The evidence shows that antibodies can be oriented and immobilized using coupling agents such as amino phenylboronic acid, which helps control antibody orientation and improve recognition efficiency [N3-F4]. Electrografting of aryldiazonium species is also used to link biosensor recognition elements to the electrode surface, enabling stable and reproducible covalent immobilization of biomolecules [N3-F4]. This means that the choice of immobilization method directly affects both specificity and signal quality [N1-F1][N3-F4].

3. **Signal generation and detection mechanism**  
   Amperometric biosensors measure current changes resulting from electron transfer reactions, typically at a fixed potential [N6-F3]. Impedimetric biosensors detect changes in impedance between working and counter electrodes, with the signal split into resistive and capacitive components [N6-F3]. Voltammetric methods are especially useful for trace detection because they can achieve high sensitivity and are effective for low-concentration analytes [N1-F1]. Overall, the sensor architecture is designed to convert a biochemical interaction into an electrochemical signal that can be measured and interpreted [N1-F1][N6-F3].

## Analytical performance characteristics

### Sensitivity, detection limit, and dynamic range  
Electrochemical immunoassays are evaluated by sensitivity, detection limit, and dynamic range. Sensitivity refers to the ability of a method to discriminate between small concentration differences, while detection limit is the minimum amount detectable with a certain level of confidence [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The literature explicitly highlights that electrochemical aptasensors can achieve tunable dynamic sensing ranges, indicating that the response range can be tailored to the target analyte [N2-R1]. For hormone immunoassays, the evidence also indicates that sensitivity can be improved by optimizing nanomaterials, recognition elements, or amplified response schemes, while noise reduction can come from hardware optimization, software processing, chemometric methods, or machine learning [N5-F2]. This means that analytical performance is not only about the sensor’s intrinsic properties but also about how it is optimized for the intended application [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F2].

### Selectivity and cross-reactivity  
Selectivity is a key performance characteristic because electrochemical biosensors can be affected by nonspecific interactions and matrix effects. The matrix effect can restrict access of redox molecules to the sensor and lower sensitivity, while nonspecific interactions can cause interference [N5-R1]. The same source also notes that the method’s limit of detection can be higher than the instrumental limit of detection because of recovery rate, matrix effects, and interference [N5-F2]. In hormone immunoassays, this means that selectivity is not only determined by the antibody itself, but also by the overall biosensor design and the matrix in which the hormone is measured [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The hormone-specific evidence further shows that cross-reactivity is evaluated explicitly, with the ACTH sensor being tested against other hormones such as cortisol, estradiol, testosterone, progesterone, hGH, and prolactin [N3-F4].

### Reproducibility, stability, and assay time  
Reproducibility is an important practical concern. The biosensor review notes that sensor-to-sensor reproducibility can suffer in comparison to chemical counterparts, and that biological samples can introduce significant noise and variability [N5-F2]. Stability is related to the sensor’s performance over time, but the evidence here is stronger on reproducibility and matrix effects than on long-term stability. Assay time is another key factor, as electrochemical biosensors are often designed for rapid detection and can be miniaturized for point-of-care or real-time monitoring [N6-F3]. The evidence also suggests that assay performance can be optimized through hardware and signal-processing approaches, which supports the idea that reproducibility and speed are not mutually exclusive objectives [N4-R4][N6-F3].

The evidence shows that estradiol, testosterone, and ACTH are each approached with somewhat different assay requirements and performance characteristics.

### Estradiol  
For estradiol, the evidence points to antibody biosensors based on competitive mechanisms and to the use of different bioreceptors, with competitive immunosensors excelling in estradiol detection [N3-R2]. Testosterone detection is reported with very low detection limits and a wide dynamic range. The sensor uses a competitive immunoassay format and oriented antibody immobilization, which helps control cross-reactivity and improve selectivity [N3-F4]. The extremely low detection limit reflects the importance of both recognition design and signal amplification in hormone detection [N3-F4].

Matrix effects are a major challenge for all three hormones. Biological samples can restrict access to redox molecules, lower sensitivity, and introduce nonspecific interactions and interference [N5-R1]. The method’s limit of detection is often higher than the instrumental limit of detection because of recovery rate, matrix effects, and interference [N5-F2]. This means that sample preparation is not merely a preprocessing step; it can significantly alter the observed LOD, selectivity, and reproducibility [N5-F2][N5-R1].
